8f13969a68ed3f91: Having agreed to new peace talks with Ukrainian and American representatives earlier this month, Russian negotiators suddenly wanted to discuss the European security order, too.
It was an obvious attempt to divert attention from the urgent need, after almost five years, for a ceasefire in Russian president Vladimir Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine.
While the inept US negotiating duo of Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff seemed to go along with the Russian proposal, the Europeans saw right through it.
They pointed out that there is already an agreed European security order, to which Russia is a signatory. The only problem is that Russia is blatantly violating it. That is what must be discussed.

The European security order is basically no different from what the United Nations Charter established in 1945. Coming after two bitter, brutal world wars, the UN Charter codified the territorial integrity of all states, and identified the crime of aggression as the ultimate violation of international law.

But the European order that gradually emerged towards the end of the Cold War went further than this. Through the laborious negotiations leading up to the Helsinki Accords in 1975, and through the process that produced the Paris Charter of 1990, Europeans added provisions on democracy, human rights, and economic cooperation to the basic security architecture.

Of course, there were occasional disagreements about how to implement these agreements’ requirements, and in both Georgia and Moldova in the 2000s, Russia openly violated provisions barring the presence of a country’s armed forces on the territory of another without its consent.

These moves sparked bitter debates, with Russia eventually calling for revisions to the European security order. The Kremlin, for obvious reasons, objected to the provisions concerning human rights and elections, and demanded that they be deleted or substantially diluted.

It wasn’t difficult to see why. A series of “colour revolutions” had started to sweep through the region, most notably in Georgia and Ukraine, where protesters demanded democratic reforms, the rule of law, and closer links with democratic Europe.
Upon returning to the presidency after a brief stint as prime minister to circumvent constitutional limits, Putin himself was confronted with huge demonstrations in Moscow.

With a democratic wave sweeping much of the world at the time, the Kremlin understood that the colour revolutions in other countries had inspired pro-democracy demonstrations on its own streets. More to the point, it knew that pro-democratic forces could count on moral support from the West.

Russia tried to force new negotiations to suppress previously agreed commitments on democracy, but no one else would support such an effort. The order that had been established at the summits in Helsinki and Paris stood firm.

More recently, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov has called attention to a provision from a 1999 Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe document, which holds that signatories “will not strengthen their security at the expense of the security of other states”.

Yet he completely ignores another provision from the same document, which reaffirms “the inherent right of each and every participating state to be free to choose or change its security arrangements, including treaties of alliance”.
Such cynical cherry picking is dishonest even by Lavrov’s standards. Membership in Nato or the European Union clearly preserves peace and in no way threatens Russia.

Democratisation in other countries may well inspire those seeking democratic change inside Russia, but that is not the democratising countries’ fault or problem, nor does it endanger Russia’s security.
Putin is now left trying to roll back various European countries’ security choices, and thus their sovereignty. This is obviously a non-starter.

Finland and Sweden chose to enter Nato not to attack Russia, but because Russia had just launched a full-scale invasion of another European neighbour. No sane person is under any illusion about cause and effect.

One hopes that at some point there will be an opening to return to confidence-building and arms-control measures. But with Russian guns blazing and Russian bombs falling over another European country’s civilian centres, now is obviously not the time.

The European security order’s foundational principle is to reject aggression and respect other countries’ territorial integrity. There is no need to revise that order, only to wait for a Russian regime that is willing to accept it.
In the next round of talks, European representatives will demand an immediate end to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. Until that happens, there is nothing else to talk about.
Carl Bildt is a former prime minister and foreign minister of Sweden.

dc93da4cf6a361d8: Over 223,700 children have dropped out of school in Cameroon’s Northwest and Southwest regions, while 2,463 schools are non-operational
Originally published on Global Voices
A general view of Buea's OIC Market in the Southwest Region of Cameroon, where displaced families sell goods to support their livelihoods. Photo by Cynthia Ebot Takang. Used with permission.

For children displaced by Cameroon’s ongoing armed Anglophone conflict, reaching safety has not ended the struggle. In Buea, the capital of Cameroon’s Southwest region, some children are balancing school with market trading to help their families survive.

“At least here in Buea, there are no gunshots, and we do not have to hide in the bush,” says 11-year-old Lorane in an interview with Global Voices, describing the relative safety his family found after fleeing their home in Cameroon’s conflict-affected Southwest Region.

The move brought the children to a calmer environment where they could resume schooling and live with less fear of armed violence. But leaving their communities also meant losing homes, familiar surroundings, friendships and, for some, years of education. In Buea, the struggle to rebuild family livelihoods has introduced another responsibility to their lives: helping their parents earn a living.
A safer place, but a childhood reshaped by displacement

The Anglophone crisis in Cameroon began in 2016, when teachers and lawyers began protesting over the perceived marginalization of English-language education and common-law systems, which they say favored French. This escalated into wider demonstrations and a government crackdown. In 2017, the situation deteriorated into armed conflict between government forces and separatist groups seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions as a state commonly referred to as Ambazonia. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) estimates that between 2.1 and 2.2 million people have been displaced due to the violence and insecurity.

At Buea’s OIC Market, children from displaced families sell bleach, puff-puff, plantains, ginger, garlic, and oranges, particularly during weekends and before school. Some travel from neighboring communities to help their parents sell goods, while others work around family-owned stalls.

For 14-year-old Joy, this means traveling from Mutengene to Buea on weekends to sell sachets of bleach. Her mother buys the bleach in bulk and repackages it into smaller sachets, which Joy sells for CFA 100 (about USD 0.17) each. She says daily sales can reach CFA 10,000–15,000 (about USD 16.81–25.21), helping support the household and her siblings.

Joy has been working since her family fled their village when she was in Class Five. “They were shooting guns in my village, so my mum had to bring us here so we could continue school,” she says. She has since become used to the routine, which allows her to contribute to the family while continuing her education.

For 14-year-old Sidoine, displacement meant losing four years of schooling. Her family fled Ekona after their house was burned while they were away at the farm. She remembers hiding in the bushes when they heard attacks were coming, unsure what would happen next. Her family eventually left their hometown, Ekona, for Buea, joining thousands of others who have had to rebuild their lives away from their roots. A well-wisher eventually helped her enroll in school in Buea.
Although the family sometimes visits their farm to collect food, it has not been possible to return permanently. Sidoine misses her former home and friends.
Rebuilding a family livelihood

For younger children, displacement has also changed family routines. Twelve-year-old Michelle sells plantains while waiting for his mother to return from church. His 11-year-old cousin, Lorane, sometimes accompanies him. The two help their parents attract customers, particularly on weekends.
They also miss people they left behind in Ekona, including their grandmother, who died during a raid as a result of the crisis.

Susan Achuagoh, a mother of five whose house was burned during the conflict, has had to rebuild her livelihood as an orange seller in Buea. She gives her children small quantities of oranges to sell while she remains at her stall. This helps supplement their family income.
“I sell oranges; I give them small things to walk around with while I stay at the stall,” she shared in an interview with Global Voices. “If they do not help like that, it will not go at all.”

Her children’s education was interrupted for more than three years during the conflict. Another mother, Mami Blessing, says her children’s schooling was also disrupted and that they now help her at the market as the family struggles to make ends meet.
The cost of conflict

Godiva Ndang epse Limene, Education and Partnerships Officer at Street Child UK-Cameroon, says the prolonged crisis in the Northwest and Southwest has increasingly become a crisis of childhood, affecting education, protection, and development.

Children exposed to armed violence, displacement, and repeated insecurity may experience anxiety, difficulty concentrating, and social withdrawal. Taking on economic responsibilities can add to these pressures. Ndang says work that takes up time needed for learning, rest, and play can affect children’s cognitive, emotional, social, and physical development.

She stresses that helping in a family business is not automatically child labor. The distinction depends on the child’s age, the nature and duration of the activity, the risks involved, and whether it interferes with education, health, rest, or development.

The right to education is only one of the rights affected. Children also have a right to rest, leisure, and play, as well as protection from economic exploitation. For those uprooted from their communities, maintaining friendships, participating in cultural life, and developing a sense of belonging are also important parts of growing up.
Learning spaces offer a route back to education

The scale of the disruption remains significant. Figures from the Regional Delegations of Basic Education cited by UNICEF in September 2026 show that 223,749 children were completely out of school in the Northwest and Southwest, while 2,463 schools were non-operational. Of these, 2,005 were in the Northwest and 458 in the Southwest.

To educate children in conflict-affected communities, local partners including TeenAlive, the Foundation for Inclusive Education (FIED), Strategic Humanitarian Services (SHUMAS), and the Authentique Memorial Empowerment Foundation (AMEF) support Mobile Neighborhood Learning Corners and Satellite Learning Corners. These are established in accessible locations such as village chiefs’ homes, churches, schools, and community verandas.

The program has supported close to 100 learning corners across the two regions. Other education interventions include help with school enrollment, uniforms, and learning materials, as well as Teaching at the Right Level, a tutoring program.

Street Child also combines education with other forms of support. Its girls’ resilience and empowerment work provides displaced adolescent girls with life skills, literacy, and vocational training, alongside start-up kits and mental health assistance. Its Play for Peace initiative, supported by the FIFA Foundation, uses sports to promote peace, health, and education in conflict-affected communities.

Ndang says children also need psychosocial support, safe learning environments, and opportunities to play and interact with their peers. She adds that helping caregivers rebuild their livelihoods matters because reducing economic pressure on families can lessen the burden on children.
Ambition despite displacement
Despite interruptions to their education and the responsibilities they have taken on, the children interviewed for this story continue to speak about their goals and ambitions.

Eliot, 14, who helps his mother sell oranges on weekends, wants to become an engineer. Sidoine hopes to study law, although she worries about the years she lost in school. Vickians, 12, who fled Lebialem and now studies computer science, wants to become a computer engineer.
On weekends, Vickians sells miondo, a cassava-based delicacy, with her parents. Her family continues to make sacrifices to keep her in school, and she remains determined to pursue her education.

At the start of the 2026–2027 academic year, Southwest Governor Bernard Okalia Bilai said the authorities wanted children across the region to have equal access to education and learning facilities, despite differences in school attendance between urban and rural communities. His remarks, reported in this September 2026 interview on the reopening of schools, underline the challenge facing the region: ensuring that displacement and insecurity do not determine whether children can access education.

Reporting note: The names used for the children in this story are pseudonyms to protect their identities. No photographs of the children have been published. Consent was obtained from parents before the interviews were conducted.
Written by Cynthia Ebot Takang

a2b0b71c81205cd4: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.

The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.

The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.

All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets.

You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure, something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder.
Thanks. Great to be here.
I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos.
I know.
It’s like a normal thing that happened.
It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash.

[Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people.

Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem.

Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!”
What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it?

I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later.

But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell.

I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good.

So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better.
Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first?

Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now.

Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that.

Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year.

I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs.

Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work?

They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw one estimate from Steve Rattner saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry.

But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today.

I was chatting with a bunch of corporate governance experts and law professors and they were all saying Anthropic, like OpenAI, has such an unusual corporate structure that they aren’t actually beholden to shareholders in the way that some public companies are. Shareholders can never vote out executives. They don’t have a lot of power to influence anything really. It’s the founders and this special trust, which we can get to in a second, that have the power.

But either way, they were all saying it doesn’t matter if shareholders have a say here really in voting. It’s about the fact that no matter who has a say, Anthropic is going to be under so much pressure to make money and to buy compute and catch up with OpenAI in that way, that this is going to be a huge reckoning for them. We’re probably going to see a lot of things fall by the wayside, maybe even some expensive safety efforts.

I want to come to the governance structure angle here. We live in a time of Nvidia scandals. Corporate governance is all the rage now. It’s the hottest topic in American business, but let’s come to that in one minute.

I just want to stay on “can you sell a token for a dollar more than it cost you to make it” for one more turn. It’s just the dumbest way of thinking about this. Anthropic rents capacity from big cloud providers, from hyperscalers. They run the GPUs in them. They pay for power, they pay for the GPUs. There’s some input cost and then they have to sell the token for more than all those input costs.

That is the dumbest way of thinking about their business. I promise you that they think about it in a more sophisticated way than that, but that is how I think about it. I was just at the Microsoft Ignite conference this week and I saw Satya Nadella and he was very clear to me and others that they’re going to try to bring the price of tokens down, that their whole system is designed to make all the AI vendors fungible underneath Copilot and they’ll pick the best model for the task and make sure you get the cheapest one for whatever it is you’re trying to do.

That seems totally at odds with what Anthropic needs to do, which is get more and more margin for every single token they sell so they can keep renting capacity from data centers or buy more chips than OpenAI or whatever it is they need to do. How are they structured to solve that problem? Is it just more people using AI or is it more expensive tokens?

I think it’s a little of both, and it’s interesting because Anthropic has been kind of sneakily trying to do this. We wrote a piece in the past year about how there was a big outcry, particularly focused on Anthropic, for passing on costs to consumers. Individuals who were customers of Anthropic were really mad because they felt like the prices were going up for the same stuff or for worse quality and that costs were just getting passed on to them.

This became a thing across the industry, a big outcry, but Anthropic bore the brunt of it. Anthropic had to have a public statement. They’re like, “Look, we’re going to work on this.” And they did roll it back a little, but I mean, they’ve got to keep doing it in some way.

The other thing they’re focused on is hoping that their models are going to be good enough that people just form an attachment — not emotionally, well maybe — but form an attachment to them and they can moat people in. They’re all about the moat these days: “We’ve got to build a moat.” OpenAI is about this, too. They want so much of your everyday life and business to be married to Anthropic’s tools that it’d be really hard to port it all over and you won’t want to and you’ll just keep paying. So that’s what they’re going for.

They’re also, of course, hoping that enterprise and government contracts are going to really make up a bunch of this, in which case you don’t have to worry quite as much about nickel-and-diming because they’ve got a lot of money. But I think that’s the interesting part here. When it comes to people that do care about the price a lot, they’re just trying to moat them in and hope for the best.

What’s interesting there is that consumers are sensitive to price in one way. I think Anthropic’s big business customers, which is where they’ve been historically focused, are sensitive to price in different ways.

If you’re paying Anthropic a lot of money, you might want to be able to switch providers quickly and you might demand data sovereignty and all this stuff that big enterprises are thinking about. Anthropic either has to deliver that, which would kill their moat for their big enterprise customers, or say, “We’re so good, you can’t have that.” I’m not sure that they can say the second one yet.

That’s why they’re marketing this safe, trustworthy AI line so deeply, because it’s the only thing they’ve really got going for them here. When you have an enterprise customer, most of the time you do have to give them data sovereignty. You can’t trade on their data. There’s a lot of stuff that Anthropic could be doing to make more money that they can’t do when someone is paying that much.

I think that’s really why they’re driving home this point of being the safe, trustworthy alternative because that’s the only thing that’s really going to get people to stick around, particularly if they also drive home the cybersecurity tools in an age when everything’s getting hacked all the time.

The other interesting thing is even not with huge enterprises, but with small to medium-sized businesses, I’ve been chatting with a bunch of them and they’ve all been creating their own internal tools to kind of track which tasks they need specifically to use an expensive Anthropic model for and which ones they can port over to maybe an open-source model or a really cheap model.

So a lot of companies like law firms — and people in a lot of different industries that have small to medium-sized businesses — are literally creating their own internal benchmarks about, “Okay, let’s save money as much as we can to just only put 10 percent of our tasks toward the expensive Anthropic model, and then this 40 percent can go to an open-source model and this 50 percent can go to a mid-tier, cheaper model.”
So that’s what’s really interesting to me. People are trying to figure this out on their own and not even sharing those benchmarks publicly because it’s their own way of budgeting.

I actually heard Nadella this week say every company will have its own set of evaluations and they will test the models against them and always use the most efficient one and this will become one of the major things that every company does.

The flip side to that is I’ve heard Anthropic executives say, “Well, you will always want the frontier model because your competitor will always be using the frontier model and if you use a cheaper one, you’ll be left behind.” And that has always seemed somewhere between naive and idealistic to me because I think a lot of companies do cheap things knowing that their competitors will also do cheap things.
I agree completely. Everyone’s being cheap.

Yeah, I think if you can get away with good enough, you’re going to find out exactly where good enough is and you will not assume that your competitor is going to eke out a 5 percent advantage by using a more expensive model. Somewhere on the margin is where all of the costs should be and the market will figure it out.
Exactly.

It just feels like the basics of the business, maybe on IPO day, the pressure isn’t on that, everyone’s just very happy and rich. The next quarter’s earnings are going to be where we start to see this shakeout. Can it keep growing the way it’s growing at the margins it needs to build everything, especially when its own suppliers are now major shareholders?
Totally. And we saw one quarter where they experienced huge growth and then the next quarter wasn’t that much. So yeah, I mean they’re going to have a lot to reckon with.

Let’s talk about the governance issues. Because of Nvidia, corporate governance is the hottest topic in American business. Like you said, OpenAI and Anthropic have some of the most complicated governance structures in history.

If you think that Anthropic’s future is to sell the best intelligence — the most capable, the most cutting-edge frontier, close-to-AGI intelligence possible — you would probably not do a bunch of safety work. You would probably not kill your margins on a bunch of researchers who are telling you to stop or slow down or not release the best model.

Anthropic is deeply committed to doing that. You and I have had conversations before about whether that can withstand the pressures of capitalism and growth. That was hard when they weren’t a public company, but now they are. Talk about Anthropic’s structure and how they’re trying to codify their commitment to safety.

Yeah, that’s a really great question. I just published a piece about this. It’s so interesting to me that Anthropic, despite seeing all the roller-coaster drama that OpenAI went through around the Sam Altman ouster and all of the restructurings that that company has gone through, Anthropic has a similarly unusual structure. And in a way it’s helpful because they’re not beholden, as we said, to shareholder pressure besides if shareholders start selling off their stock or don’t buy more.

But the two kinds of groups of people that have power over what happens at Anthropic are the founders and this group called the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT). Anthropic likes to market this as being like, “Oh, don’t worry about that the founders are doing what’s best for humanity but with no checks. We’ve got this trust above us that can appoint or remove us anytime.” As we’ll see in the movie Artificial, Sam Altman famously says, “Oh, well, the board can fire me whenever.” He says that a million times.

Now, Anthropic is implying the same thing: “Oh, we have this trust above us. They can remove or appoint the majority of board members,” even though it’s actually not all of them, but we’ll get to that in a minute. So this trust is a group of right now four people and none of them have a lot of AI experience. It’s [former Federal Reserve Chairman] Ben Bernanke, a foreign policy analyst named Richard Fontaine, an experimental physicist named Christopher Stubbs, and a former GiveWell executive named Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT.

I spoke to a couple of former Anthropic employees that left not too long ago and one of them said that this trust is kind of handpicked to not rock the boat at Anthropic. The founders appointed them. They’re not going to be appointing someone that’s going to probably disagree with them a lot.

Ironically, the trust doesn’t have the authority to step in on everyday decisions at Anthropic, unlike even the OpenAI nonprofit board that existed. They could say, “Oh look, don’t release this model. It’s too dangerous.” The trust doesn’t have any of those powers. All it can do is appoint or remove certain board members. Even then, they have to give 30 days’ notice to a small committee of the board, which includes Daniela Amodei, the chair of that little committee who is also a founder of Anthropic.

To oversimplify things, out of these seven board seats, the trust gets to pick three, the founders get to pick three, and then the kind of tie-breaking seat, the seventh one, the trust technically appoints, but they have to basically get founder approval to do it. So it’s one of these things that’s so complex, but when you really look at the nitty-gritty of it, the founders have pretty unchecked control here. I think that’s something that’s getting lost in the narrative of, “Oh, this trust is above us. Don’t worry.” Okay, well, they don’t really have much power to check you.

The founder control structure is the wildest thing I have ever read about in years of doing the show and thinking about business. Anthropic has seven founders. They have been issued a single share of stock that holds 50.1 percent of the voting power of the company. That is issued to a company called Founder LLC, and they’re the seven co-owners of Founder LLC.
How on earth does that work? Do they just all get together and then decide how to vote the one share of stock?

61f2e8252c946f4b: My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?"

It's a great question! They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn got salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted.

If you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike.

AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds.
But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?"
Easy: it did.
Everything breaks, all the time, including the narrative

AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are currently smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed.
But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most important region, us-east-1.

At 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud). The all-clear showed up at 6:53 AM.

Every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS said in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. I do think it's patently unreasonable to blame them for this specific problem; "acts of war" are kinda hard to predict from the corporate planning meeting.
A few things combined to help AWS out on November 15. First, it was pre-dawn Pacific time on Sunday. Most of us slept through it; my kids aren't even up that early.
Further, the services that were most impacted (IAM Identity Center) were for engineers signing in to AWS accounts, not consumers staring at an app that stopped working.

Plus, the competition sucked all the oxygen out of the room: a day-plus Microsoft 365 364 outage and a four-hour nationwide air traffic ground stop had done a great job of level-setting what kind of outage was going to get attention, and "us-east-1 being weird but the apps still work" doesn't cut it.

Downdetector – which is owned by Accenture, so it's not like AWS doesn't have a throat to choke if they want to stop picking on reporters – measures consumer screaming. Originally, it was largely Twitter semantic analytics. This isn't a bad thing! As I said, I want to know if the internet is breaking. We can sort out exactly what part later.
The November 15 outage didn't produce that kind of screaming. Ironically, the tool that AWS is complaining about in the newspaper is the reason they skated by without notice on this outage.
Counterintuitively, Downdetector reports that outages have decreased since about 2022. Instead, what we're seeing is large-scale centralization.

Our companies don't run email systems internally anymore; we outsource to large technology companies who are almost universally better at fixing and resolving large-scale issues than we will be internally. And it feels unkind to dunk on those hard-working folks for their outages; would we want them to dunk on us for ours?
("Wait, don't you own stop.lying.cloud?" "Do as I say, not as I do.")

But whether anyone notices depends upon what layer broke, and when. If my company's email system broke on Monday, and your company's email system broke on Tuesday, the story would stop at "computers suck." But when everyone's email system goes down at once, the world takes notice.

Microsoft had to tell the whole world about a bug it mostly sat on since July. AWS hasn't had to tell anyone anything. My editor runs a tech publication that covers this stuff for a living and didn't know. You can't buy PR like this, and AWS didn't have to.
If I were AWS, I'd stop complaining about Downdetector and send it a fruit basket. ®

954fc3aa085f664d: BRUSSELS: The chairman of European Union leaders proposed further cuts to the European Commission's draft EU 2028-2034 budget on Saturday and suggested new revenue streams for the EU, including a digital tax, to help finance EU policies.

The cuts proposed by Antonio Costa, who chairs summits of EU leaders, would reduce the overall seven-year budget by €40 billion to €1.582 trillion compared to a proposal presented by the Irish EU presidency in October and by €180.6 billion compared to the original Commission proposal.

Costa's proposal mainly cuts the European Competitiveness Fund — aimed at helping make European industry more competitive against China and the US — defence and external spending. Money for agriculture and cohesion is relatively protected compared to the Irish compromise proposal.

Nevertheless, France criticised the new numbers as not sufficiently protecting farmers, and the European Parliament's chief budget negotiator, Siegfried Muresan, said the numbers were a step backwards.

"This proposal is unacceptable to Parliament and cannot form the basis for our consent. The EU budget is an investment budget. Cuts, more cuts and a side of cuts are not an investment strategy," he said.

EU leaders will discuss Costa's proposals at a special summit on Nov 26-27 with a view to narrowing differences between the EU budget's net contributors and net beneficiaries, and to reaching an agreement in December.

The EU budget is how the 27-member bloc finances all its policies — from supporting farmers to developing new technology and supporting industry and research against competition from China and the US.
It also covers student exchanges, equalising standards of living across the EU, help for Ukraine and EU officials' salaries, among others.
Digital tax a proposed new revenue

The EU budget is financed from national contributions and the so-called "own resources" — taxes and levies that are collected by EU countries but are dedicated to the EU budget, such as customs duties, a percentage of value-added taxes or a tax on non-recycled plastic waste.
The more such "own resources" the EU budget has, the less governments have to contribute from national coffers.
Costa's proposal for the digital tax builds on a 2018 proposal by the European Commission that was not taken up by EU governments at the time.

Costa has now proposed that the EU put a 3% tax on the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data for companies with an annual turnover for digital activities of €50 million in the EU and a global turnover of over €750 million.

This would mean taxing mostly US-based digital giants such as Google, Microsoft, Meta, Apple or Amazon, a move many EU governments have been wary of for fear of angering US President Donald Trump, who has spoken against such a tax.

To find more money, Costa proposed slowing down the repayment of the capital of the more than €600 billion that the EU will have jointly borrowed by the end of 2026 for its post-pandemic recovery fund.

The repayment of the interest and capital will start in 2028 and last until 2058 as initially planned, but the repayment of capital may be slower in the first seven years to leave more money in the budget for other priorities, officials said.

The budget and its sources of revenue must be agreed unanimously and it is often an acrimonious battle. The seven-year ​2028-2034 budget under discussion now is particularly difficult because of additional pressures on national ⁠budgets from high energy prices and defence spending.

Although the EU budget only has to be ready for 2028, leaders want a deal by the end of 2026 because there are elections next year in France, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia, ⁠Finland ​and Slovakia, with the budget likely to play a role in electoral ​campaigns.

639db76df47d5053: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 21 — In an increasingly competitive food and beverage industry, the use of instant ingredients and commercial pastes has become a common choice among food operators, particularly to save preparation time and reduce costs.

However, Banglo289, a restaurant serving traditional Malay cuisine from various states, has chosen to go against the grain by using fresh ingredients and traditional cooking methods to preserve the authenticity of its dishes.
The restaurant also offers a unique dining concept, combining an upscale and comfortable setting with prices aimed at the mid-market segment.

“The idea behind setting up this restaurant actually stemmed from our observation of a gap in the market for traditional food, particularly Malay cuisine, served in a comfortable setting at reasonable prices.

“Usually, if customers want to enjoy this type of food at affordable prices, roadside stalls are their best option, but the surroundings may not be very comfortable. If they prefer a more comfortable setting, there are exclusive restaurants, but they have to pay premium prices,” its Chief Executive Officer Shareen Farzida Sukri told Bernama.
Making heritage cuisine accessible

Banglo289 seeks to bridge that gap by offering an exclusive dining environment and a wide selection of dishes, allowing customers to choose their preferred food and portions according to their tastes and budgets.

The Kelantan-born entrepreneur from Kuala Krai said the average spending of between RM30 and RM50 per person per visit recorded by the restaurant did not refer to the fixed price of any particular dish, but rather the total amount customers typically spent during each visit.
“This includes a combination of rice, side dishes, vegetables, porridge, desserts, fruits and traditional cakes, all reflected in a single bill,” she explained.
The menu also varies according to dining hours, with different selections available for breakfast, lunch and dinner.
Recounting the restaurant’s establishment in 2022, Shareen Farzida said that, as its name suggests, the premises occupy a century-old bungalow located along Jalan Raja Chulan here.
Within four years of operation, the restaurant brand has expanded to four outlets at different locations across the Klang Valley, with plans to open more branches in other states nationwide.
Balancing costs and business sustainability

The expansion has also brought greater responsibilities, particularly in ensuring that the concept and quality of food remain consistent across all outlets, a task Shareen Farzida acknowledged posed challenges, especially in terms of costs.
Using fresh ingredients, including spices, requires employees to prepare basic ingredients themselves, such as fresh chillies, onions and turmeric.
“The cost of fresh coconut milk alone reaches RM50,000 a month for all our outlets. We adopt this approach to ensure the authenticity of our food.

“Previous generations, such as our mothers and grandmothers, rarely or never used instant ingredients, possibly because of preservatives and chemicals that could affect the original taste of the dishes,” she said.

To demonstrate its commitment to preparing basic ingredients from scratch without relying on instant pastes, the restaurant has incorporated open-kitchen concepts near the serving counters at almost all its outlets, allowing customers to observe the cooking process firsthand.
Minimising food wastage
Shareen Farzida said rising raw material prices were managed through careful operational planning to ensure that the restaurant did not compromise on food quality.

“Among the cost-saving measures we have introduced are those that do not affect the taste of our food, such as opting for simpler decorations and food presentation that are not overly elaborate but remain neat and visually appealing.

“We also focus on improving workforce management by arranging staff shifts and allocating duties according to peak and off-peak hours, ensuring productivity remains high without placing an excessive burden on salary costs,” she explained.
The restaurant also prioritises efficient raw material management, with each outlet having its own purchasing team to source fresh ingredients according to the respective kitchen’s requirements.
“Raw ingredients must be used on the same day and cannot be kept for use on another day.

“We have adopted this approach to minimise wastage and keep our overhead costs under control. This is why dishes are prepared in stages and in small batches of only about 10 to 15 servings at a time, with no leftover dishes kept for the following day.
“If a particular dish is in high demand, additional portions can be prepared as long as operating hours and the availability of raw ingredients permit,” she said.
She added that the restaurant sometimes had to explain its concept to customers, particularly its practice of preparing food in controlled quantities to maintain quality and prevent wastage.
Nevertheless, she said certain best-selling dishes, such as smoked beef cooked in coconut milk with bird’s eye chillies (daging salai masak lemak cili api), were always made available to customers.
Traditional cooking
To preserve the authenticity of its traditional dishes, Banglo289 also takes the initiative to learn heritage cooking techniques directly from their original sources.

Banglo289 Business Development Director Datuk Mohd Hafidz Safari Ramli said research teams, usually comprising between six and 12 chefs, travelled to selected states, including Kelantan, Pahang, Negeri Sembilan and Johor, to meet veteran cooks and local communities who still possessed knowledge of traditional food preparation.

“This research is an ongoing learning process. Each visit is not merely about obtaining a list of ingredients, but also understanding the entire process, from selecting raw materials and determining measurements to the sequence of cooking steps and the time required to produce an authentic dish,” he said.
He added that the teams would revisit the original sources if their attempts to recreate a dish did not meet the desired characteristics, whether in terms of taste, colour or texture.
Every recipe and cooking method learnt is documented as a reference for the chefs, helping to ensure consistent food quality even when dishes are prepared by different individuals.

Citing Kelantan’s nasi dagang as an example, he said the team not only learnt its preparation methods directly from local sources in the state but also sourced ingredients, including spices, from there.

For patin fish cooked in fermented durian paste gravy (patin masak tempoyak), the research team travelled to Temerloh, Pahang, to understand the balance of sourness and the distinctive consistency of the gravy.
Meanwhile, the preparation of smoked beef in coconut milk with bird’s eye chillies involves manually smoking the meat over rambutan wood and coconut shells for approximately eight hours.

“All these are part of the preparation process that cannot simply be bypassed. If we want to preserve our cultural heritage through food, we must do it properly and uphold the true meaning of the word ‘heritage’,” he said.
Reviving endangered heritage dishes

Apart from preserving the authenticity of traditional dishes that remain familiar to the public, Banglo289 is also committed to reviving heritage cuisine that is becoming increasingly difficult to find, particularly dishes that are no longer widely prepared by restaurant operators or younger generations.

Shareen Farzida said the initiative, known as ‘Endangered Recipes’, stemmed from her team’s observations of the diversity of traditional food in several locations, including dishes that were known or still prepared by only a handful of food operators and elderly cooks.
Among the dishes identified for preservation are lemang periuk kera, kulat sisir masak lemak, lawar terung and bubur anak lebah, each with its own distinctive ingredients and preparation techniques.

Citing bubur anak lebah as an example, she explained that the traditional sweet delicacy, made from a rice flour-based batter, requires considerable manual skill and a special mould to shape tiny pieces resembling baby bees before they are cooked until chewy and served with sweet coconut milk gravy.
Preparing such unique dishes requires patience and direct guidance, as the techniques cannot necessarily be mastered through written recipes alone, she said.

She added that the team’s visits to several states had also uncovered dishes that were prepared only during Ramadan or certain festive seasons, limiting opportunities for younger generations to discover and learn how to make them.
This has raised concerns that the knowledge and skills involved could disappear if those who still possess them pass away before having the opportunity to pass them on.

“That is why we plan to collaborate with Yayasan Hasanah, an impact-driven foundation under Khazanah Nasional Berhad that actively supports the preservation of local arts, heritage and culture, to fund the production of a special documentary on this ongoing project.

“Heritage cuisine is not merely a cultural treasure to be printed on a menu. It is a body of knowledge and a cultural identity that must continue to be cooked, savoured, documented and passed down properly, without shortcuts,” she said. — Bernama

ce467387ca06079a: From Jonathan Edward
The narrative surrounding Chinese industrial overcapacity is being used as a convenient scapegoat for domestic economic stagnation.

The recent comment by Mazli Noor, China’s overcapacity, a test of Malaysia’s resilience, exemplifies this point by suggesting that Malaysia must erect trade barriers, tighten anti-dumping regimes, and mandate local content rules to shield domestic producers from Chinese imports misses the fundamental mechanics of global trade.
If Malaysia wishes to thrive, it must either compete on the same terms through aggressive state-backed industrial policy or pivot towards producing different, higher-value goods and services.
Attempting to insulate uncompetitive industries behind regulatory walls is not a strategy for resilience, but a guarantee for economic obsolescence.
'Overcapacity' is a politically loaded talking point
The very term "overcapacity" is a politically loaded construct designed to frame superior manufacturing efficiency as a market distortion.

In April 2024, former US Treasury secretary Janet Yellen warned that Chinese industrial overcapacity threatened global markets and Western workers - a claim China rejected, crediting its export success to market forces, scale, and supply chain integration rather than unfair manipulation.

State support has undeniably played a major role in China's industrial ascent, yet there is nothing stopping Malaysia from adopting similar measures if it genuinely wishes to dominate heavy industries like crude steel.
If replicating China’s state-capitalist model is neither fiscally practical nor politically desirable for Putrajaya, then market forces must be allowed to dictate the outcome.
The failure of domestic protectionism

Malaysia already knows the consequences of coddling legacy industries. For decades, protectionist policies and selective state support have benefitted a handful of well-connected conglomerates without translating into broader economic dynamism.
Instead, these sheltered entities have repeatedly devolved into sluggish, uncompetitive monopolies that pass higher costs onto Malaysian consumers and downstream businesses.

It is an uncontroversial local reality that shielding domestic firms from foreign competition removes the very pressure required to innovate. Calling for anti-dumping duties and stricter customs hurdles will merely entrench inefficiency while penalising every Malaysian household and manufacturer that relies on affordable inputs.
Moving up the manufacturing value chain

Trying to compete head-to-head with the world’s largest manufacturing powerhouse on basic commodities like crude steel or bulk plastics is economic suicide. Rather than lamenting low capacity utilisation in legacy blast furnaces, Malaysia must upskill and upgrade its industrial base.

Modern manufacturing technologies, such as precision computer numerical control (CNC) machining, industrial 3D printing, and advanced metallurgy, allow smaller, agile firms to produce specialised components and bespoke widgets made from exotic materials.

Instead of churning out raw base stock, Malaysian manufacturers should be supplying precision-engineered parts for global aerospace, medical devices, and specialised equipment for the regional oil and gas sector.
Unlocking agriculture, aquaculture, and services

Malaysia’s economic future does not depend on matching China factory for factory when vast domestic sectors remain chronically underutilised. Consider agriculture and aquaculture, both of which possess immense export potential. For years, prime agricultural land has been squandered on speculative property developments that sit unsold, or cleared under questionable pretexts for logging.

Meanwhile, our rivers suffer from heavy sedimentation caused by upstream deforestation, alongside rampant chemical pollution and garbage dumping. Properly managed, Malaysia’s waterways could anchor a lucrative freshwater aquaculture export industry.

Malaysians are an inventive and entrepreneurial people. We have even successfully bred sturgeon in tropical conditions to produce luxury caviar. Imagine what could be achieved if environmental stewardship and agricultural land reform were treated as national priorities.

Similarly, Malaysia holds substantial natural advantages in high-value services. With a multilingual workforce and established legal and financial frameworks, the nation is well-positioned to expand aggressively into regional tech support, fintech, cross-border legal services, and financial advisory. Competing in brainpower and service delivery bypasses the physical scale advantages of Chinese manufacturing entirely.
Geopolitical hypocrisy and trade realities

Singling out China for its industrial might also ignores the broader geopolitical reality facing Southeast Asia. The US has swung towards unpredictable unilateralism, weaponising tariffs and imposing sweeping restrictions on artificial intelligence chips and advanced technologies. Its actions in the Middle East have kicked off the energy crisis the whole world is reeling from.

At the same time, the European Union is grappling with severe deindustrialisation and has become an increasingly cumbersome trade partner, imposing stringent regulatory barriers that directly threaten Malaysia’s environmental sovereignty and palm oil exports.

Why, then, should Malaysia lecture China for being a cost-effective manufacturer and a vital trading partner when we do not publicly chastise the US for its tech blockades or the European Union for its protectionist green mandates? Criticising the one major power that still possesses the capacity to produce at scale and low cost while offering a massive consumer market for Malaysian exports defies basic economic logic.
Adaptability over obstruction

Complaining about how well-resourced the competition happens to be reflects a defeatist mindset. True progress comes from pulling oneself up, not attempting to drag a competitor down. If Malaysia wants to empower local industry, it should immediately deregulate sectors where bureaucratic red tape suffocates enterprise, slash corporate and manufacturing taxes, and provide agile firms with the land, energy, and capital needed to scale.
Trying to restrain China’s industrial output is an exercise in futility, and attempting to freeze market dynamics is like trying to stop time itself.

Global manufacturing is constantly in motion. When a dominant power shifts its focus towards new frontiers, nimble competitors step in to fill the vacated space. Malaysian manufacturers must embrace this reality, pivot away from lost battles in heavy commodities, and capture the specialised, high-value niches where they can genuinely win.
Jonathan Edward is a media practitioner and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
e337f75878c782e6: MUNICH, Nov 21 — Bayern Munich’s star striker Harry Kane pledged to return for the “business end of the season” after undergoing surgery on his left ankle today.
Kane limped off after 20 minutes of Bayern’s 1-1 home draw with Cologne in their Bundesliga match yesterday, the club confirming the England captain had torn a ligament in his ankle.
Bayern issued a statement today saying the Ballon d’Or winner had “successfully undergone surgery” on his left ankle.
“The 33-year-old will now begin his rehabilitation programme,” Bayern said, with the injury expected to keep Kane out for three to four months.
Kane posted a picture on social media from his hospital bed today, vowing to work his way back to fitness this season.
“The highs and lows of life! Obviously very disappointed to get this injury but as always it’s an opportunity to show resilience and improvement going into 2027.
“I’ll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season.”
Kane shared a quote from three-time Super Bowl-winning wide receiver Julian Edelman: “tough times don’t last, tough people do”, while thanking his supporters for their messages of support.
Kane has a history of ankle issues although he has only missed a handful of games since moving to Bayern in 2023.
England coach Thomas Tuchel will be keeping a keen eye out on how England’s most capped player’s rehabilitation progresses.
England play Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals in late March.
The injury comes at a difficult time for Bayern, who are currently missing several players, particularly up front.

Bayern are without Luis Diaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and captain Manuel Neuer, while midfielder Jamal Musiala and coach Vincent Kompany both returned after long lay-offs yesterday. — AFP

His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).

These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.

These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that dive-bombed our ancestors, brightened the sky, recalled an old tune, and got hosed by marine mucus.

First, scientists discover that eagles are hunting large baboons, hinting that early human relatives once sated ancient avian appetites. Then: star-on-star contact, a musical memory lane, and the secrets of cetacean snot.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
Eagle-eyeing you…for dinner!
Hobaiter, Catherine et al. “Signs of Eagle Predation on a 22-kg Adult Primate.” American Journal of Biological Anthropology.
Death came from the sky for early humans, according to a new study that suggests giant eagles preyed on our ancestors far more recently than was previously known.

Birds of prey (raptors) have hunted primates for at least 20 million years, including early human relatives, known as hominins. For example, a hominin toddler known as the “Taung child” shows signs of being killed by a raptor roughly 2.5 million years ago. But scientists have assumed that hominins outgrew their status as bird bites since that time, and there are no reports of raptors preying on primates that weigh over 28 pounds on record—until now.

In 2025, scientists discovered that Verreaux’s eagles—one of the largest eagle species in the world—at Ennedi Plateau in Chad are likely hunting adult olive baboons weighing up to 57 pounds. The team found baboon remains among the region’s sandstone cliffs that show signature marks of eagle predation, such as talon punctures on the skull and scrapes to the shoulder bones.

“We cannot definitively rule out scavenging activity, but the severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip,” said researchers led by Catherine Hobaiter of the University of St. Andrews. The team also observed the baboons rapidly retreat when eagles approached, suggesting that they feared aerial attacks.

Some researchers have argued against the “raptor-mediated predation” of the Taung child on the grounds that the hominin would have been too heavy for a bird. The study’s authors get extra points for including a quote from the comedy Monty Python and the Holy Grail on this point: “It is a simple question of weight ratios. A five-ounce bird could not carry a 1-pound coconut.” IYKYK.

However, the laughs stop there, as the team refutes this idea by recounting the grisly “low flight with sustained grip attack” that eagles perform on ungulates, such as antelopes or cattle, which reveal that raptors can kill animals that are many times their own weight with the right approach.

“Briefly, an eagle will land on the back or neck of a moderately large ungulate, gripping it firmly with its talons. If the prey withstands knocking to the ground, the eagle will ride it with wings outstretched and flapping to maintain balance until the quarry collapses, either from exhaustion, shock, or internal injury. A similar tactic is described in the extraordinary report of a Harpy eagle (Harpia harpyja) attacking a 52-kg adult woman.”

Wow, new fear unlocked! Imagine being an early hominin, minding your own business banging rocks together or something, when suddenly a giant bird of prey either pushes you off a cliff or rides you to death. For everyone preparing to eat a huge bird for Thanksgiving next week, be grateful that it’s no longer the other way around.
In other news…
A union made in heaven
Karambelkar, Viraj et al. “An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion.” Nature.
Speaking of unwieldy meals, scientists have captured an unprecedented glimpse of a star eating another star, thereby forming a new mega-star.

Over the past few years, scientists noticed that something weird has been unfolding in a binary star system called AT 2025abao—nicknamed “Bao” (yum!)—in the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, which is about 2.5 million miles away from the Milky Way. One of the stars, “Big Bao,” was expanding into its dying red giant phase, which pulled its companion, “Little Bao,” into a deadly spiral. Last year, the system rapidly brightened, signaling that Big Bao had swallowed Little Bao.

“In October 2025, the star underwent a dramatic eruption” and exhibited “a sudden increase in its photospheric temperature to about 8,000 K,” said researchers led by Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University. The system “shows the defining hallmarks of luminous red novae, a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection…during the merger of a star with its companion.”
“This inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly,” the team noted.
Congratulations to the newly-fed couple! Long may Bao shine.
Girl, put your records on / but don’t think you own that song
Turnbull, Cara et al. “Music illuminates sociocultural dimensions of autobiographical memory.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

We’ve all had that feeling of hearing a familiar song and being transported to a specific time and place in our lives. But as it turns out, the recollections stirred by those cherished songs are probably not all that special, according to a new study that surveyed 233 undergraduate students about these so-called “music-evoked autobiographical memories.”

The students (aged 18-23) listened to clips of 32 popular songs grouped into two categories: “new” songs released from 2014 to 2019, during their adolescence, and “old” songs released from 1985 to 1995, before they were born. When asked to reminisce about the songs, students with similar backgrounds were remarkably aligned in their answers.

“Memories evoked by country songs were more strongly associated with very recent time periods (college) and themes relating to family, driving, summertime, romantic partners, and listening to music (particularly music selected by someone else),” said researchers led by Cara Turnbull of Texas Tech University.

“Alternatively, memories evoked by hip-hop songs were most often associated with friends, acquaintances (such as classmates, coworkers, and teammates), dancing, and being at school, while those evoked by pop songs were most associated with middle school, listening at home or by oneself, and singing along,” the team added.

As an elder millennial, it was humbling to realize what counts as an “oldie” these days. I also felt my generation’s soundtrack was done dirty by offerings like “Achy Breaky Heart” by Billy Ray Cyrus or “Whoomp! There it is” by Tag Team. No Stevie Nicks? Madonna? Wu Tang? All I ask of future generations is that you do not judge us solely by the croonings of C+C Music Factory and Bryan Adams, I beg you.
Thar she blows (DNA)!
O’Mahony, Éadin et al. “Breath to Genome: Whole Genome Sequencing of Large Whales From Blow Sampling.” Molecular Ecology Resources.

Join hands, dear friends, for we are about to run directly through majestic fountains of whale snot. Scientists who flew drones through whale “blow”—the mucus-filled vapor exhaled by whales through their blowholes—have successfully sequenced whole genomes from the snotty samples, representing “a major step towards non-invasive cetacean sampling,” according to a new study.

“Preserving biodiversity requires the genetic monitoring of wild populations, which is traditionally done through invasive sampling techniques for DNA collection,” said researchers led by Éadin O’Mahony of the University of St. Andrews. “However, this approach can impact animal welfare or be impossible to implement due to behavioural responses to anthropogenic factors or national/international legislation.”

Indeed, I think that we can all agree that humans have stressed whales out enough as it is. Instead of invasive biopsies of skin and flesh with darts or scrapers, O’Mahony and his colleagues equipped drones with petri dishes and flew them through a total of 58 blows from 26 Northeast Pacific humpback whales in the Gitga'at First Nation territory of northern British Columbia.

The team “established that a whole humpback whale genome can be recovered from exhaled respiratory vapour (‘blow’), marking a significant methodological advancement in non-invasive cetacean genomics.”
While it’s not the kind of blow most people associate with breathing orifices, it just might be what we need to study whales without hassling them.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.
7da468e8fb51d357: If you’ve ever wondered how small an instance of ChatGPT could get, wonder no longer. Someone has actually rigged up a tiny version of the chatbot to run on a Super Nintendo cartridge.

Tech journalist and retro tech enthusiast Benj Edwards is responsible for ChatGPT for SNES. He's published it online running in an emulator, complete with SNES-era music and sound effects, and for download as an SNES ROM, too.

It’s not a big model, mind you, and performance is thus pretty limited: According to the website, it’s a 2.2 million-parameter offshoot of OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-120b, which was used to develop its training conversations – so in that sense it truly is a ChatGPT that runs on an SNES cartridge. Edwards described it to The Register as a distilled version of the aforementioned open-weight model.

There are two options built into ChatGPT for SNES: One that’s purely the model, with every word generated coming right from its tiny little silicon brain, and another that includes a fact book culled from the opening sentences of around 150,000 simple English Wikipedia articles. If you opt to run both versions and ask it the same questions, you’ll notice a massive difference.

Given some of the other responses we got while testing, there’s really no good reason to run the base model – memory isn’t really an issue given the basic build is about 4MB and the factbook build is just 19MB.
Edwards admits that it’s not the most helpful AI model, either – this is just an experiment after all.

“It is not a useful assistant: the model is millions of times smaller than the models behind ChatGPT, knows about 8,000 words, and often gets things wrong, sometimes confidently,” Edwards noted in his writeup. In that sense, it really is vintage AI on vintage hardware. “The fact book can carry mistakes too.”

If you have an SNES lying around (lucky you), you can download the ROM from this link. If you want to get it running on an SNES you’ll need a cartridge that allows running of custom ROMs, and that supports Nintendo’s Super FX graphics coprocessor. Cartridges like the FXPak Pro and SD2SNES support it. The factbook version also requires support for the aftermarket Media Streaming Unit 1 (MSU-1), which adds CD-ROM like features to the SNES. MSU-1 is available in both of the flash carts mentioned above.
If you have some real hardware skills, however, you could technically make your own ChatGPT cartridge.

“The ‘pure’ version, which generates all responses from the AI language model, could run from a real custom SNES cart,” Edwards told us – it doesn’t even actually need the Super FX chip. “I do have a version of ChatGPT for SNES that can run without the Super FX chip, but without the extra processing power the answers are not as good.”
That said, Edwards believes its absolutely crazy and nonsensical answers are part of the fun.
“ChatGPT for SNES can definitely make mistakes too, but it's almost cute when it does it because of its limited knowledge and its playful interface,” Edwards told us.

While a human may have designed the experiment, the coding work was done by AI, Edwards told us – he’s been interested in it since the 1990s and is pursuing more experiments with tiny AI models using the help of the bigger ones.

“I've been theorizing about what I call ‘tiny talking machines’ … over the past year,” Edwards told us, and he’s been able to use coding agents to turn those ideas into actual software. ChatGPT for SNES is one example, and he also created an NES ROM called Séance that uses an even smaller AI model able to run on an original Nintendo Entertainment System that simulates talking to a ghost in a haunted game cartridge.

“I designed the scope of what the software should be, how it should work broadly, what chip it should use, how the interface should look and work, and the sounds it makes when it types responses,” Edwards told us. He added that he sees the project as an AI/human collaboration, which is where he believes AI works best.

“The AI agents who did the coding for this project currently advise that we've hit the limit of how good the AI model can be on the limited hardware,” Edwards said - he’s not taking their word for it, though. “It's up to human creativity to transcend those assumptions. I have already come up with new ideas that I believe can make a tiny model like ChatGPT for SNES even more coherent, and I'm working on them now.” ®

398d974c87825819: BRUSSELS, Nov 21 — The EU put forward plans to tax the world’s biggest digital companies to fund its next budget today, as it seeks to bridge divisions among member states over the bloc’s long-term funding.

European Council President Antonio Costa unveiled a new spending proposal that slashes by €204 billion (RM919 billion) a plan initially put forward by the European Commission, which some countries had slammed as too onerous.
“I believe this proposal can bring us closer to a final agreement,” Costa told a press conference in Brussels.
EU countries have been squabbling over the size of the next budget, with Germany leading calls for major cuts after the commission last year proposed a €2 trillion budget for the 2028-2034 period.
Berlin criticised a revised proposal published last month that suggested slashing the bloc’s future seven-year budget by €140 billion.
Costa, who represents the EU’s 27 states, is seeking to reach a deal by the end of the year balancing contributions from member states with new sources of revenue for the bloc.

Among these could be a tax on digital firms that the draft Costa presented today says will concern companies with an annual turnover for digital activities of at least €50 million in the EU as well as a global turnover of more than €750 million.

They would be subjected to “an annual contribution corresponding to 3 per cent of the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data”, according to documents shared by the council.

The plan is likely to provoke US President Donald Trump’s ire since his administration has reacted angrily to EU fines and moves against Big Tech under its content and competition rules in recent years.
The draft also includes plans for a levy on electronic waste and higher tobacco taxes.
Parliament threat
The document will be at the centre of hours of fraught talks when EU leaders meet in Brussels next week.

Costa is pushing for a deal in December, amid EU fears that a delay would push talks into a fraught election year in 2027 with worries about what potential eurosceptic victories in France and elsewhere would mean for future dealmaking.
Once EU states find an agreement, they will have to negotiate with parliament — a task that also promises to be difficult.
Key budget lawmaker Siegfried Muresan warned the EU Parliament would block the spending plan if member states continued to ignore its concerns.
“We think that the debate... is focused too much on cuts,” he said this week.
Germany is part of a grouping with five other so-called “frugal” EU members, including Sweden, which expressed scepticism this week over new taxes.
“It’s money taken from somewhere else. It won’t solve the financial equation,” Swedish Europe Minister Jessica Rosencrantz said.
“The focus should be on the expenditure side, where the volume needs to go down” and the national contribution “needs to go down”, she added on Thursday.
Costa does not only have to contend with the frugals’ demands.
France, the second-biggest EU economy and a net contributor to the budget, argues the bloc needs sufficient means to match the rising challenges it faces.

Meanwhile, 17 countries from southern, central and eastern Europe have formed a group known as the “Friends of Cohesion” and are pushing for greater funding to support agriculture and regional development. — AFP
