He said that following the information, police officers moved to the Batu 3 area, Jalan Pahang, near Tapah, to conduct a surveillance and the vehicle involved was successfully detected at about 5.30 pm.
“The police instructed the driver of the vehicle to stop for inspection, but the driver failed to comply with the order and instead sped off, nearly hitting the on-duty police officer.

“The police officers then gave chase to the vehicle all the way to the Tapah toll plaza area. In an effort to intercept the suspect’s vehicle, the police vehicle’s bumper was hit by the suspect’s vehicle,” he said in a statement today.
Mohd Fadzil said another police vehicle from the Ipoh district police headquarters joined in the chase before the suspect’s vehicle was successfully intercepted at Simpang Pulai.
He said all four suspects were arrested, and the vehicle they used was seized.
According to him, the initial investigation found that all those detained were teenagers and the results of the urine screening tests showed that they were all drug-free and had no previous records.

“The three teenage boys who were detained have been remanded for four days starting today, while a teenage girl was granted police bail as she is involved in an ongoing investigation in Jitra, Kedah,” he also said.
He added that the case is being investigated under Section 186 of the Penal Code as well as Section 279 and Section 353 of the same code. — Bernama
9ae1a487f014aa02: ATHENS, Nov 21 — Greece’s prime minister has come under fire for asking youngsters whether they’d like the mature-content Grand Theft Auto VI videogame for Christmas.
“Which of you will ask for Grand Theft Auto VI as a Christmas present from grandad and grandma?” Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in a TikTok post yesterday, with the game’s logo briefly flashing on-screen.
“We all know that grandfathers and grandmothers rarely say no to their grandchildren,” he added.
The post was designed to promote a €400 (RM1801) pension bonus from Mitsotakis’ government, as it faces elections next year.
But it came under attack from critics calling it inappropriate to encourage minors to buy a mature game.
“The prime minister ‘promotes’ a video game that is banned for minors just to follow the trend,” the main opposition socialist Pasok party said.
Leftist daily Efsyn called the move a “gaffe” while conservative newspaper Dimokratia said it was a “tragic” error.
Ironically, Mitsotakis’ government has joined a growing number of countries imposing curbs on young people’s use of social media.
Like its predecessors, GTA VI is an open-world action game in which players roam freely through a sprawling city, stealing cars, pulling off heists and carrying out missions for criminal gangs.
Containing intense violence, gore, sexual content, nudity, strong language and drug and alcohol use, it has an age rating of 17 or above.
Coming after a 13-year hiatus in the series, the game has been a smash hit worldwide, raking US$3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day according to its publisher Rockstar Games. — AFP
710f310d7fd86fab: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 21 — US rock band My Chemical Romance (MCR) drew nearly 130,000 fans across its two Kuala Lumpur concerts at the TM National Stadium in Bukit Jalil on November 19 and 20.

In a post-event statement today, organiser Hello Universe described the Kuala Lumpur concerts as the band’s biggest shows of its Southeast Asian tour, marking the culmination of almost 18 months of anticipation following the initial announcement and subsequent postponement.
The organiser also said the two-night event demonstrated Malaysia’s capacity to host large-scale international rock concerts.
It added that bringing MCR to Kuala Lumpur was no small undertaking, citing overwhelming ticket demand, the postponement and the logistical challenges involved in staging the shows.
“The two nights meant far more than live music for tens of thousands of loyal fans who held on to their tickets and waited patiently.
“They offered an opportunity to reconnect with the songs that shaped their teenage years, brought back cherished memories and fulfilled a long-held dream,” Hello Universe wrote in its statement.
The first night drew 62,000 fans, while the second and final night saw 63,000 emo fans flood the stadium.
MCR performed The Black Parade in its entirety during the first half of both concerts, delivering the songs through an elaborate theatrical production featuring stage actors and an opera singer.

The production was set in DRAAG, a fictional authoritarian state where MCR assumes the identity of The Black Parade, and incorporated the mythology of MOAT, a reconditioning facility where the band’s characters are held captive.
The second half of both concerts saw the award-winning band perform B-sides and hits from its other albums, including ‘Helena’, ‘Demolition Lovers’ and ‘I’m Not Okay (I Promise)’.

Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, who attended the first concert, previously said the shows brought wider economic benefits to the city, with international visitors making up 40 per cent of the first night’s audience.

He said the influx of overseas concertgoers contributed to the local economy through spending on accommodation and car rentals, among other things, describing the economic spillover as “very positive”.

ce25ea90419308e2: HANYU (Japan), Nov 21 — Tens of thousands of mascot fans gathered in a city near Tokyo today to meet and greet more than 200 life-size cuddly characters that promote local towns and businesses.
In the land of Hello Kitty and Pokemon, mascots are used to promote everything from prison to railways to private businesses, and popular ones gain full-on celebrity status.
“This is the first time I’ve ever come to an event like this, so I’m kind of excited,” Yuriko Okamori, 51, told AFP at the annual meetup event.
The mascot meetup has been held in the city of Hanyu since 2010 and nearly 220 mascots were invited to join this year, according to organisers.
On a stage, a troupe of animal mascots danced to upbeat pop music as a large crowd filmed them on smartphones and clapped along.

Elsewhere, a popular pony mascot representing Gunma prefecture was surrounded by fans eager for selfies, while a cat mascot was pushed through the packed crowd on a cart to make its way across the venue.
City official Shogo Dei, who oversees the event, said 80,000 people attended the two-day meetup last year and that organisers expect a similar turnout this year.
“These local mascot characters representing regions are part of Japanese culture. Our aim is to help revitalise towns across Japan through these characters,” Dei told AFP.
Mascots in Japan can generate millions of dollars in revenue if they become successful, even without the global recognition of major intellectual property brands such as Pikachu.

Another popular character, Hikonyan, a samurai helmet-wearing cat mascot associated with Hikone Castle in western Japan, has helped draw tourists to the area. The character even received around 10,000 New Year’s greeting cards from across Japan this January.
“There are so many different characters representing different places, and it’s not uncommon to see even adults carrying mascot goods on their bags,” Okamori said.
“I think that’s something uniquely Japanese.” — AFP
48bc4937a718bdc3: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 21 — The Ministry of Education is looking into the need to increase the number of assistant wardens and guidance and counselling teachers to ensure students receive optimal attention and support while staying in hostels.

Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek said the aspiration of parents to see their children gain admission to fully residential schools should be balanced with the children’s own abilities and emotional readiness.

“As we plan for our children’s future, it is important that we also listen to their voices and understand their feelings. Our dreams as parents must align with our children’s own abilities and emotional readiness,” she said in a Facebook post today.

Earlier, she said that she had held discussions with the police in Kuala Kangsar, Perak, on strengthening the safety and well-being of students residing in the hostel of the educational institution concerned.

The discussions covered compliance with standard operating procedures, hostel management, and the importance of parents assessing their children’s level of readiness before sending them to boarding schools.

Fadhlina said every child had a different level of adaptability, with some adjusting quickly while others required more time, adding that some children were able to cope well with academic competition, while others needed greater encouragement.
As such, she stressed the importance of creating an environment where children could share their thoughts and be heard without being judged.
“I want parents to know that we share the same hopes. We want our children to succeed, but more importantly, we want them to grow up safe and happy,” she added.
She also advised parents not to be overly concerned if their children do not gain admission to their dream schools, as every child has his or her own unique path and timeline for achieving success.
“Most importantly, regardless of where they study, they must know that our love and acceptance never depend on the name of their school or their examination results,” she added. — Bernama
c6df213692ff58e9: BRUSSELS, Nov 21 — The European Union is weighing a tax on the world’s biggest digital companies to fund its next long-term budget, with the measure set to be included in a new spending proposal to be published today.
That will likely provoke US President Donald Trump’s ire since his administration has reacted angrily to EU fines and moves against Big Tech under its content and competition rules in recent years.

EU countries have been squabbling over the size of the next budget, with Germany leading calls for major cuts after the European Commission last year proposed a two-trillion-euro budget for the 2028-2034 period.
Berlin slammed the draft proposal published last month that suggested slashing the bloc’s future seven-year budget by €140 billion (RM633 billion).
EU lawmakers warned this week that the cuts went too far, setting the stage for difficult negotiations.
But even before that, member states must agree among themselves.
European Council chief Antonio Costa, who represents the EU’s 27 states, will unveil his draft oday, which several sources told AFP would propose cutting the budget by €200 billion.
Part of the budget will come from new sources of revenue and Costa is due to propose a tax on digital giants, also pushed by the European Parliament.
Costa will then host a meeting of EU leaders on Thursday and yesterday, who will likely dissect his budget proposal during a Brussels summit set to be stormy.

The commission already put forward plans for a tax on large companies, a levy on electronic waste and higher tobacco taxes. The expectation is the digital tax will replace the levy on large companies.
EU lawmakers also want to tax cryptocurrencies and online gambling, which the parliament estimates could raise 32 billion euros annually, including the digital levy.
Parliament threat
Key budget lawmaker Siegfried Muresan warned the EU Parliament would block the spending plan if member states continued to ignore its concerns.
“We think that the debate... is focused too much on cuts,” he said this week.
Germany is part of a grouping with five other so-called “frugal” EU members, including Sweden, which expressed scepticism this week over new taxes.
“It’s money taken from somewhere else. It won’t solve the financial equation,” Swedish Europe Minister Jessica Rosencrantz said.
“The focus should be on the expenditure side, where the volume needs to go down” and the national contribution “needs to go down”, she added on Thursday.
Costa does not only have to contend with the frugals’ demands.
France, the second-biggest EU economy and a net contributor to the budget, argues the bloc needs sufficient means to match the rising challenges it faces.

Meanwhile, 17 countries from southern, central and eastern Europe have formed a group known as the “Friends of Cohesion” and are pushing for greater funding to support agriculture and regional development. — AFP
d6648099dae6a691: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 21 — Five Bumiputera companies successfully listed on Bursa Malaysia between April 2025 and September 2026, said Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir.
The companies are Orkim Bhd, which was listed on the Main Market, and SumiSaujana Group Bhd, Elsa Bhd, GTA Holdings Bhd and United Asiapac Energy Bhd, which were listed on the ACE Market.
Akmal Nasrullah said the listings demonstrated the potential of Bumiputera enterprises to grow, attract investment and gain access to broader capital markets.

“Our next challenge is to build on this progress by enabling more Bumiputera enterprises to scale up, compete in higher-value industries and become market leaders,” he said in his opening remarks at the YP Leadership Conference 2026 here today.
He highlighted that under the 13th Malaysia Plan, Malaysia aims to raise its economic potential while raising the floor of living standards.
“The Bumiputera Economic Transformation Plan 2035 complements this direction by advancing meaningful Bumiputera participation, ownership and competitiveness.
“Human capital development is fundamental to both agendas, but it must be closely linked to enterprise growth and economic opportunities,” he said.
“This is where the complementary roles of Yayasan Peneraju, the Bumiputera Agenda Steering Unit (Teraju) and Ekuiti Nasional Bhd (Ekuinas) become especially important.
“Together, their mandates support an ecosystem that develops talent, strengthens enterprises, facilitates business expansion and promotes long-term economic ownership,” he added.
He said Yayasan Peneraju identifies and nurtures high-potential talents to become value creators in professional, business and community spheres.
Meanwhile, Teraju supports the development and expansion of Bumiputera enterprises, while Ekuinas contributes through investment, business transformation and long-term value creation. — Bernama
bf49764d74c2b57f: TEMERLOH, Nov 21 — The Pahang government has allocated RM450,000 for a programme to control the redtail catfish population, which has been identified as a potential threat to the state’s native fish population if left unchecked.

Pahang Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Wan Rosdy Wan Ismail said the programme, being carried out simultaneously at seven locations statewide, including Pekan and Jerantut as well as Temerloh, was aimed at reducing the population of the invasive fish species.
He said the redtail catfish was a predatory alien species that could threaten the survival of other native fish species sharing the same habitat.
“The state government takes the issue of redtail catfish very seriously as this is an alien species that can threaten existing fish populations.
“If left unchecked, it could wipe out native species because it is highly aggressive and preys on other fish, eventually becoming the dominant species,” he said.
He was speaking to reporters after officiating at the Pahang 1st: Tawan Baung Ekor Merah Fest programme at Dataran Pekan Sehari, Kuala Krau, here today.
Wan Rosdy said one of the programme’s activities was a redtail catfish fishing competition to encourage members of the public to catch as many of the fish as possible.
He expressed hope that the initiative would help reduce the population of the species and protect native fish from the threat of extinction.
Meanwhile, Wan Rosdy said the Pahang government would provide assistance to federal civil servants in the state in the form of goods or non-cash contributions under the state budget tabled yesterday.
He said the approach was adopted in view of the state government’s financial constraints in providing cash assistance to the large number of federal civil servants. — Bernama
5a2cddb29de54880: BRUSSELS, Nov 21 — Two economists, one French and one German, are to join the European Central Bank’s top body, the EU said yesterday, which suggests the two heavyweight nations might have reached a deal on the bank’s next chief.
The ECB is the central bank for the 21 countries that use the euro, setting interest rates that influence borrowing costs across the economy, from mortgages to credit-card repayments.

European leaders have been locked in negotiations for weeks to ensure a balance between the interests of the biggest powers at the institution, with ECB chief Christine Lagarde announcing in October she would step down next February.

France’s Laurence Boone and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier are the sole candidates to fill two vacant seats on the ECB’s executive board, said Kyriakos Pierrakakis who heads the Eurogroup of eurozone finance ministers.
Running unopposed the pair are set to become the bank’s next market operations head and chief economist.
This settles part of a major reshuffle at the central bank for the 21-nation euro area, leaving only one major outstanding piece: the name of Lagarde’s successor.
France is believed to be supporting Spain’s former central bank head Pablo Hernandez de Cos for the top job, while former Dutch bank chief Klass Knot is also in the running.
The nomination of Brunnermeier and Boone to the board suggests France and Germany might have reached a deal to install Hernandez de Cos.
Once France and Germany have decided on their choice, they will have to win the backing of the other nations, although they are likely to support the decision of the eurozone heavyweights.
The ECB’s governing council and European Parliament also have to give their blessing. — AFP
ca2a900cfaf72f38: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 21 — The Ministry of Economy has outlined four strategic priorities to support the healthcare reform agenda under the 13th Malaysia Plan, focusing on healthcare investment, financing sustainability, industry and talent development.

Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir said the priorities would complement the Health Ministry’s role through national development planning, resource prioritisation and cross-sectoral coordination.
He said the first priority was aligning healthcare investments with population needs, taking into account access to services, avoidable delays, workforce availability and operational resources.

The second priority was to strengthen healthcare financing sustainability by exploring the establishment of a national health fund and a strategic purchasing platform, as well as enhancing public-private collaboration in selected services, including diagnostic imaging, elective surgery and virtual specialist consultations.

“The Reset Strategy addresses pressures on private healthcare costs, including through price transparency and insurance reform. A key initiative is the base medical and health insurance and takaful plan, with market introduction targeted for early 2027.

“These efforts should complement the public healthcare system. Cost containment should never come at the expense of clinically appropriate treatment,” he said when officiating the 35th Malaysian Urological Conference (MUC) 2026 here today.

Also present were MUC chairman Dr Arvind Vashdev Jagwani, newly elected Malaysian Urological Association (MUA) president Dr Toh Charng Chee, and KPJ Selangor consultant urologist Prof Datuk Dr Khairul Asri Mohd Ghani.

Akmal Nasrullah said the third priority was to develop healthcare as a high-value economic sector, particularly in medical devices, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, digital health and clinical research, with efforts focused on moving beyond importing and using technology towards developing and commercialising more Malaysian solutions.

He said the fourth priority was to strengthen healthcare talent and professional capabilities, including training capacity, staff retention, geographical distribution and the mix of specialist skills.

Meanwhile, Akmal Nasrullah said prostate cancer cases recorded in the Malaysia National Cancer Registry Report 2017-2021 increased to 6,441 from 4,189 in the 2012-2016 period, with 63.3 per cent of cases for which staging information was available diagnosed at Stage III or IV.
He encouraged the MUA to contribute to evidence-informed policymaking by sharing data on waiting times, treatment outcomes and patient-reported quality of life. — Bernama
63bd0caf8c884812: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 21 — Jamie Oliver joined Robert De Niro on The Graham Norton Show last night with a story about cooking for the actor 30 years ago, when a plate of pasta came back to the kitchen at London’s River Cafe.

0de2c219b0451986: NEW DELHI, Nov 21 — At least 11 people have died and more than 180 have been hospitalised after drinking suspected tainted alcohol in India’s north-eastern state of Manipur.
The victims fell ill after consuming the liquor, Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh said in a statement yesterday.
“Over 180 patients have been admitted in the two hospitals so far, while the death toll has reached 11 in the last 48 hours,” the statement said.
He also ordered an enquiry into the incident, saying those responsible would be arrested and punished.
Deaths from illicit or adulterated alcohol are regularly reported in India, where cheap liquor sold outside regulated channels can contain methanol, a highly toxic industrial chemical.
In May, at least 15 people died after drinking methanol-laced illicit liquor in Pune and neighbouring Pimpri-Chinchwad in the western state of Maharashtra.
In August, 13 people died and more than 60 were affected after consuming methanol-tainted liquor in Gujarat’s Bhavnagar district, according to local media reports.
Such liquor is widely consumed across India, where a bottle is sometimes sold for less than a dollar. If ingested, methanol can cause blindness, liver damage and death in larger concentrations. — AFP
7ebdc050516c1af3: GENEVA, Nov 21 — Countries opened a path today towards finding an international agreement on regulating lethal autonomous weapons systems — though campaigners seeking to stop so-called killer robots were disappointed by the “weakened” outcome.
After five gruelling days of talks at the United Nations, which dragged on into overtime, states agreed on building some form of pact over the next two years.

However, with warfare being radically transformed by artificial intelligence, non-governmental organisations wanted far swifter, legally binding rules on handing power over human life and death to autonomous machines.

With full consensus required for any decision, talks at the UN’s Review Conference of the Convention on Conventional Weapons in Geneva finally concluded at nearly 4.45am (0345 GMT/11.45am Malaysian time) today.

The 128 countries party to the convention “agreed to launch the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems, which should be conducted over the next two years”, conference president Julien Thoni told reporters afterwards.
While a majority of states want a legally binding agreement, countries that have the technology, including the United States and Russia, are reluctant to have their hands tied.
Two-year timeline
The process ahead should flesh out “which weapons can be forbidden according to international humanitarian law, and which is not forbidden but can be regulated”, Thoni told AFP.
The Swiss diplomat said the parties would work on the instrument, and then decide on whether it should be a treaty, along with the extent to which its provisions should be binding.
He stressed that having the world’s major military powers agreeing to work towards an instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS) was a big step forward.
Brazilian ambassador Frederico Meyer described a balancing act as “some countries have the power, some countries have the majority”.
Before midnight, during a break in talks, delegates spent a long period huddled tightly around Russia’s representative.
Later, a group of 15 delegates broke out for hushed talks on a staircase.
Diplomats inside could be seen pointing at amended text on the screens and refuelling on packets of crisps.
‘Watered down’
Campaign groups said the outcome fell well short of expectations.
Once activated, LAWS are capable of selecting and attacking targets without any human intervention.
According to Stop Killer Robots, a global coalition of more than 300 organisations, such systems have already been tested or deployed, including during the war in Ukraine.
“States adopted a watered-down mandate that fails to chart a clear path towards a legally binding instrument,” said the group.
“Over 95 states expressed their support for a treaty. In the final hours, a small number of states weakened the mandate introducing uncertainty about the legal status of the final document.”
Diplomacy lagging behind technology
Verity Coyle, the deputy director for arms at Human Rights Watch, said the outcome “does not provide the urgent action needed to agree new rules — but the technology is racing ahead”, she said.

Rain Liivoja, a director of the Asia-Pacific Institute for Law and Security, said the decision was one “nobody wanted but everyone could grudgingly live with”, adding that consensus merely “makes everyone equally unhappy”.
“It remains possible — likely, even — that there will be no treaty by the end of 2028,” he added.
UN disarmament chief Izumi Nakamitsu said getting an instrument completed in two years was a “very compressed timeframe” which would require “a lot of negotiations”.
She said countries should start thinking as soon as Monday about how to get as strong an instrument as possible to ban and regulate LAWS.
“The consequences of not having a strong instrument are very clear,” she told reporters.
She said a group of governmental experts from the countries would make recommendations on the legal nature and specific form of the instrument, including whether it should be a binding protocol.
“The path to, or possibility to, have a legally binding instrument is still open,” she insisted. — AFP
cbe0a917939fc064: KUCHING, Nov 21 — Caretaker Deputy Premier Datuk Amar Douglas Uggah Embas has hit out at the Democratic Action Party (DAP) over its criticism of the Sejingkat Bridge, dismissing claims that the project would force Pending Port to close and cause job losses as malicious allegations.

He said the criticism failed to take into account the Sarawak government’s wider plans for port infrastructure, recalling how opposition figures had gone to the opposite riverbank to record videos criticising the project.
“They sarcastically claimed that the Sarawak government had made a mistake in constructing this bridge because Pending Port would close and people would lose their jobs.
“That is why these people never appreciate what we have done,” he said when delivering his welcoming speech at the official opening of the Sejingkat Bridge here on Friday night.
Rejecting the claims, Uggah maintained that Pending Port would remain operational, pointing out that the bridge’s 26-metre clearance would allow most cargo vessels to continue passing beneath it.
He said the critics had also failed to recognise that caretaker Premier Tan Sri Abang Johari Openg had wider plans for Sarawak’s port infrastructure, including the construction of a new port.
Uggah further pointed out that facilities for roll-on/roll-off vessels at Senari Port had been completed, with capacity to accommodate up to 3,000 vehicles at a time.
“The GPS government has plans, unlike DAP, which only knows how to blame others. These are malicious allegations,” he said.

The impact of the Sejingkat Bridge on Pending Port had previously been raised by Sarawak DAP chairman Chong Chieng Jen, who questioned restrictions on vessel access and whether Senari Port had sufficient capacity to accommodate additional cargo traffic.
The Kuching Port Authority had earlier maintained that Pending Terminal remained operational despite concerns over the bridge’s impact on shipping activities.

Turning to the state’s infrastructure development record, Uggah said the Sarawak government had demonstrated its ability to deliver major projects despite earlier scepticism over its bridge-building programme.
He said 21 of the 22 major bridges under the programme were being implemented by the Public Works Department Sarawak at a combined cost of RM6.55 billion, while another bridge was located in Lawas.
All the projects, he stressed, were funded using Sarawak’s own financial resources.

Recalling criticism when the programme was first announced, Uggah said the completion of major crossings had transformed road connectivity and reduced reliance on ferry services, particularly along the Kuching–Miri route.
“Today, travelling by road from Kuching to Miri no longer requires taking ferries. Ferries are now a thing of the past. They belong in museums.
“This is a gift from GPS and the Premier to the people of Sarawak,” he said.

Uggah also credited Abang Johari’s leadership with strengthening Sarawak’s financial position, enabling the government to undertake major infrastructure projects and introduce initiatives such as free tertiary education.
He said Sarawak’s revenue had increased from RM5.9 billion in 2016, with the state targeting RM15.01 billion next year.

Citing these development achievements, Uggah urged Sarawakians to remain united and continue supporting Gabungan Parti Sarawak and Abang Johari’s leadership in the coming state election, saying the state’s development agenda remained unfinished. — The Borneo Post
3f29ab1519ee921a: SINGAPORE, Nov 21 — Several content creators in Singapore have been promoting a gambling site operating under the guise of a Pokemon trading card platform.
Since September, at least 10 influencers have posted videos on their social media pages promoting the website of the operator based in Malaysia.
The influencers include a former talent from local platform SGAG and an actress who was previously on Crimewatch.
The Straits Times (ST) is not naming the operator to prevent more people from using the site, which features mystery box gambling mechanics that flout Singapore’s remote gambling laws.
Users are offered virtual packs containing a virtual trading card, which the operator claims corresponds with an actual physical card.
These are known as Oripas (original packs), which are seller-made blind packs marketed as a low-cost chance at high-value cards.

Sellers often repack cards of varying values into blind mystery packs sold at a premium, with claims of high-value chances that are difficult to verify. Ultimately, buyers often end up with cards worth far less than what they paid.
ST has reported on the rampant proliferation of Oripas in the trading card community here.
The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) previously said those who sell Oripas may be committing gambling offences.
Singaporeans targeted
In the case of this Malaysian operator, it has set up a page dedicated to Singapore users, selling them virtual Oripas for between 100 and 1,200 credits a pack, with each credit costing S$1 (RM3.19).
It accepts payments via PayNow.
The website shows that in the first week of November, its top user in Singapore spent over 220,000 credits on 1,970 Oripas.
The platform also features a buyback option, where gamblers can immediately sell their prizes back to the platform for credits.
Such a mechanic is banned in Singapore, applying to games at amusement centres and funfairs to prevent gambling inducement.
The platform did not respond to ST’s request for comment.

Under the Gambling Control Act, those who conduct unapproved games of chance and lotteries can be jailed for up to seven years and fined up to S$500,000 for a first offence, with up to 10 years’ jail and up to a S$700,000 fine for a repeat offence.
Those who induce individuals under the age of 18 to gamble can be jailed for up to six years and fined up to S$300,000.
It is also illegal to promote or advertise unlawful gambling activities, even if these are based outside of Singapore. Offenders can be fined up to S$20,000.
Responding to queries about the site and the influencers involved, a spokeswoman for the Gambling Regulatory Authority (GRA) said it is aware of their activities.
She said: “We are taking steps to regulate such activities with conditions stipulated by GRA. More details on the regulation of mystery boxes are expected to be made known around end-2026.”
They did not know
When contacted, several content creators from Singapore immediately took down their posts, saying they were unaware the site was promoting gambling.
A content creator who did not want to be named said he was shocked to learn about Oripas.

He said: “When this client contacted me, I thought it was just to promote Pokemon trading cards, which are just a cute hobby. It didn’t occur to me there was this Oripas thing, which I only just found out about.”
The local influencer made two videos in partnership with the platform and was paid several thousand dollars a video.
He said he had contacted the client to end the partnership, and would be more careful with who he works with in future.
“I’ve previously said I would never promote gambling. I would never have worked with this platform if I had known what it really was,” he added.
Three of the influencers who promoted the platform are managed by DU Media.
The agency’s chief executive, Kelvin Tan, better known as Mayiduo, said the Malaysian company had approached its content creators to promote its website.
He said his team understood the brief as a trading card campaign which included pack openings.
He said: “Unfortunately, they were unfamiliar with the potential regulatory concerns associated with Oripas, and we did not identify these concerns during our pre-production review.”

ac7a4c098ff81d22: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 21 — No fancy trisuit, no flashy sporting gear — just seven hours, 19 minutes and 57 seconds of sheer determination.

Affectionately known as Pak Cik Ariffin, the veteran endurance athlete completed the gruelling 113km challenge on Saturday, finishing 391st among 587 competitors overall.
Wearing his trademark modest attire, Ariffin crossed the finish line after swimming 1.9km, cycling 90km and running 21.1km, proving once again that appearances can be deceiving.

His running performance was particularly impressive, clocking two hours, 54 minutes and eight seconds for the half-marathon distance — the fourth-fastest time among the 14 competitors in his age category.
And he did it all without the expensive trisuit commonly associated with the sport.
Ariffin’s unassuming appearance once again attracted attention on social media, particularly among Malaysians who remembered his previous barefoot running exploits.
“Remember Pak Cik Ariffin, who became famous during the TNU trail event? Today, he’s doing Ironman 70.3 Langkawi. No fancy trisuit,” Threads user @adizuh wrote.
But behind the modest appearance is an athlete who has already demonstrated an extraordinary appetite for endurance challenges.

Last month, Ariffin, from Jerantut, Pahang, became an unlikely internet sensation after completing the demanding 30km Malaysia Taman Negara Ultra (MTNU) barefoot in seven hours, 32 minutes and 36 seconds.
He finished 72nd among 326 participants, navigating muddy jungle trails and challenging terrain without running shoes.
He also reportedly cycled approximately 100km to reach the event before taking on the gruelling course.
His preparations for Ironman were similarly unconventional.
According to Stadium Astro, the first-time Ironman 70.3 competitor trained by swimming in a fish pond and incorporating cycling into his daily routine, including journeys to the mosque.
His latest achievement has drawn admiration from social media users, although some pointed out that his simple appearance should not be mistaken for a lack of financial means.
“Remember, this uncle is no ordinary man. Just look at how much the Ironman 70.3 entry fee costs. And he hasn’t even shown us his bicycle yet,” commented @punkjunks before the competition..
Others praised his determination to compete while maintaining his modest style of dress.
“Competing in an Ironman while maintaining modest dress. Excellent, uncle! May you be an inspiration to athletes everywhere,” wrote @mfzmki.
Ironman 70.3, also known as a half-Ironman, covers 70.3 miles (113km) across three disciplines, testing athletes’ physical endurance and mental resilience.

56b4c092930898f6: It's been a bad few weeks for technology on and off the planet, as NASA reported problems with its Perseverance Mars rover and Odyssey orbiter this week.

For Perseverance, the problem seems to be a relatively straightforward communications issue that has paused science operations because of low data rates. The Odyssey orbiter, however, is facing an issue that could end the mission.

The 2001 Mars Odyssey reached orbit around Mars in October 2001 to search for evidence of water and ice on the surface. The mission was supposed to last two and a half years, but the spacecraft's operations have been extended for a quarter of a century.

In that time, it has had its fair share of ups and downs, including the failure of one of its four reaction wheels in 2013. Three reaction wheels are needed to orient the spacecraft; otherwise, it must fall back to its hydrazine thrusters.

Earlier in November, between the 4th and 6th, Odyssey dropped into safe mode, which engineers determined was caused by one of the remaining reaction wheels stopping spinning. Science data stopped flowing as the team worked to recover the component; the good news was that the wheel moved when commanded. The bad news is that if the thrusters need to be used, only a few months of fuel remain.

More bad news is that the spacecraft is part of NASA's Mars Relay Network, and was responsible for sending back the first post-landing images from the Phoenix lander and the Spirit, Opportunity, and Curiosity rovers. Its loss (should it come to that) would therefore be keenly felt.

In the event the orbiter is indeed approaching the end of the road, the European Space Agency's Mars Express (MEX) and Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) could pick up some of the load although, as a former ESA insider put it: "MEX is a science mission that can do relay where TGO is a relay mission that also does science." According to NASA, TGO already sends the most relay data from Mars to Earth.

The challenge facing the Perseverance trundlebot is one of communication. On October 30, the rover's main computer detected problems with the primary radio (a series of "heartbeats" from the device did not arrive as expected) and automatically switched to a redundant backup, placing itself in a protective safe mode.

So far, so expected. Engineers brought the rover back from safe mode, analyzed the data, and made an unpleasant discovery. The backup radio was not performing as it should – it was operating at approximately half of its expected power output.

Both radios were therefore deemed inoperable – at least until the team has got to the bottom of the issues – and the rover has used X-band communications over its high-gain antenna to talk to Earth ever since. The problem here is that the connection provides a significantly lower data rate, meaning science and instrument operations are on hold.
Engineers are working first to return the backup radio to operational status, then to address the primary. ®

4d98effdc3566e59: The dominant Nepali food narrative overlooks the diverse regional histories and culinary traditions of Indigenous communities
Originally published on Global Voices
Timu khole, wild mushroom soup. Photo by Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

Food enriches our soul. It makes us who we are. However, the emergence of cosmopolitanism and global and local food politics has sidelined Indigenous food, not to mention the traditions and rituals associated with them.

“Over the last decades, ever since the country was opened up to the outside world in the 1950s, in search of a national food identity, the staple daal bhaat, a nutrient-dense combination of lentils and rice accompanied by vegetables, has been elevated to Nepal’s national dish,” writes Binti Gurung, a food historian and founder of Natural Roots Foundation, an organization dedicated to documenting, preserving, and promoting Indigenous Himalayan food heritage, traditional recipes, and local knowledge in Nepal. “The national food narrative that is being set completely obscures the varied regional histories and food practices of the Indigenous peoples.”
The Foundation, established in 2017, promotes the many varieties of food that have become neglected in Nepal, especially the plants and herbs that can be foraged in the forests and mountains.

Working with Aama Samuha, a collective of women’s groups set up to maintain cultural traditions and support communal activities in Nepali villages, she has been documenting and archiving the food knowledge primarily held by Indigenous women in Nepal.

The Lekhali Cookbook, authored by Gurung, draws its name from lekh, the high ridges in Nepal, and highlights the rich food tradition shared by women’s groups from Nepal’s Mustang, Manang, Lamjung, and Gorkha districts.
Sanjib Chaudhary of Global Voices caught up with Binti Gurung to talk about her work on food heritage. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Sanjib Chaudhary (SC): Can you introduce yourself and tell us a bit about your work?

Binti Gurung (BG): Before talking about the food heritage of Nepal, it’s necessary to mention that knowing the broader political and historical context of the country is important because a lot of what my work looks into connects with understanding of the past.

The pivotal moment can be attributed to the 1950s, when the absolutist regime came to an end. As a country, Nepal had remained closed off to the outside world for so long that very little was understood about Nepali society, particularly its food practices.

Within this environment of reaching out to the past events that happened in this land, uncovering the stories of the people, and mainly breaking down and deconstructing the idea of “Nepali-ness,” lies the understanding of our food heritage.

I myself come from what used to be called a Gurung country until the 1970s. I know something about our collective history as Gurung people, and that my great-grandfather on the maternal side was a mukhiya, a tribal chief somewhere in that Gurung country. There are no written documents about our lineage, apart from the knowledge that remains in the tongue. I take pride in that, but it also means some knowledge has not been transmitted.

My paternal grandfather was the first person to be educated because of his connection to British India, after which he did a lot in his village, which included donating some of his personal land to the village school. Whereas I am the first in my family to go to university, learn English (like the rest of my generation), and read history.
SC: Food sovereignty is a burning issue for Indigenous peoples. Can you give us an overview of what challenges Indigenous communities in Nepal are facing with regard to food sovereignty?

BG: Even though the constitution of 2015 has given recognition to the right to food, how does it translate to the many Indigenous groups accessing their food? Are the Indigenous peoples who have been living by the rivers and the forests able to access the foods that they have learned to process, collect, and eat?

For the communities that still live in or near the forest, how are their relationships affected when forests are turned into national parks? Do the Indigenous peoples who have been relying on these ancestral food practices have access? Can the state recognize and permit it?
When we start to think this way, we go beyond the conversation about food sovereignty because then we have to talk about the land and the peoples who inhabit it, and their connection to it.
The author in conversation with women's group members. Photo via Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

SC: Nepal is a multi-ethnic country, and communities have their own food and agriculture systems. However, food politics is prevalent, with some communities claiming a particular dish as solely theirs. What’s your take on this?

BG: I think it is impossible to claim any particular dish as solely belonging to only one community. After all, we live in a shared world. We are beings in constant interaction with the land. Like any living practice that is evolving, our food practices are also in motion; it is not a static, fixed thing.

What may be helpful is to think about how a dish or food practice evolved. Or even to try to understand how it has evolved the way it has, including the factors of influence. Even though we think of Nepali communities having their own food systems, if we look underneath somewhere, we can find some similar practices.

One example is the way food is harvested from the forest; this particular practice, whether in the high mountains, hills, or the Terai, remains similar. Of course, how this practice is treated by those not practicing is an entirely different thing.

SC: It’s high time we promote Indigenous food in a global space. Can you tell us about your recent book “The Lekhali Cookbook: Indigenous Food Heritage from the Highlands of Nepal” and the dishes you’d like to share with a wider audience?

BG: This book has been in the making for a very long time. When I started doing this work in 2017, at some point it felt very urgent to understand the issues around it, and gradually it became important to start documenting in a written way because a lot had been unknown.
The cover of The Lekhali Cookbook. Photo by Sanjib Chaudhary. Used with permission.

There may be many factors why the conversation around food heritage has remained so obscure, but one that I attribute strongly to is our own political history that has shaped the Indigenous experiences.

For many Indigenous communities, the problem has also been due to others writing about their history. Of course, there are some very rare scholars who have done a fine job, but in the case of our own history, there is now an immense effort to establish or re-establish our origin account. It’s very saddening to have to read about some of these accounts. And then there is also the process of verifying and fact-checking, and that takes a lot of time.

The Lekhali Cookbook came into being due to a generous grant from the British Council. A lot of the work had been conducted prior to receiving the grant, but it allowed us to visit the villages in the central Himalayas and work with aama samuha [translated as “mothers’ groups,” acting as local women’s collectives] who are heavily involved in the food production process. Based on the consultation with the groups, we collected the recipes of the eight villages of Lamjung, Manang, Mustang, and Gorkha.

In the book, we have some unique recipes that many people do not know, such as the foraged panyu (wild rhubarb), kru (yak sausage), yak curry with satu, or farsi ko bhat eaten with sattu up in the high Gorkha hills.
SC: What do you think the future of Indigenous food will look like in a decade's time? What should Indigenous communities, in your opinion, do to preserve and promote their food heritage?

BG: I think we have immense challenges ahead of us. Every year, these challenges seem to be only growing more and more. We only have to look at the recent disasters; it’s quite terrifying for the people who are living in these landscapes.

For several reasons, it’s crucial that we recognize that our situation is changing and that it is very fragile, and we have to be alert to this changing situation. So much has already changed, and within this framework we have to think of how we are going to adapt to our new circumstances, whether it is living in the city, establishing a relationship with urban life, learning to operate in a language that is not your mother tongue, learning technology, issues of sustainability, and so on.

In the midst of this vast change from our previous ancestral way of life, how are we going to hold ourselves as people with a distinct way of living, language, and culture? Moreover, how are we going to maintain the values that have been passed down to us from our ancestors? How willing are we to work for our collective welfare to protect our cultural and food heritage in this sea of change? Because without addressing these questions or without internalizing them, we cannot have real progress.
Written by Sanjib Chaudhary
